text:
Research supports testing the objective independently of residual depth, but does not establish gains for this NextItNet benchmark. [Sampled-softmax analysis (2024)](https://wujcan.github.io/papers/tois-ssm.pdf) highlights the importance of temperature and negative sampling: overly concentrated gradients can let a few difficult negatives dominate. [Scalable Cross-Entropy (RecSys 2024)](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/5392aca9-0bae-4176-9b3a-a8165957ba26) approximates sequential-recommendation cross-entropy using informative catalog subsets, reporting substantial memory savings while retaining recommendation quality. These motivate efficient multi-negative training without changing the NextItNet backbone.

Sampling correction depends on the actual proposal distribution. [Correcting the LogQ Correction (RecSys 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331) shows that conventional in-batch correction overlooks the positive’s guaranteed inclusion; its refined objective accounts for that distinction. Popularity-based or in-batch negatives therefore require careful treatment rather than blindly subtracting the same log-probability from every candidate. Separately, [improved sampled-rank estimation (2024)](https://research.google/pubs/improved-estimation-of-ranks-for-learning-item-recommenders-with-negative-sampling/) demonstrates benefits from correcting sampling bias for WARP and LambdaRank.

Hardness does not establish that an unobserved item is a true negative. [UFNRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116) explicitly studies this problem, although its teacher-based implementation falls outside the requested single-model experiment. Practical inference: first compare the baseline objective against moderate multi-negative sampled softmax with uniform sampling; then separately test temperature and conservative hard-negative selection. Exclude padding, the target, and observed training positives without consulting held-out labels. Keep one trained NextItNet per category and select solely by fixed macro validation HR@10; stronger training separation alone provides no evidence of held-out improvement.
